- Largest on-demand asset pooling provider in India's supply chain management sector based on the number of pooled Assets, according to the F&S Report; the DRHP describes the industry as one with high barriers to entry, typically characterised globally as a monopoly or duopoly within individual countries.
- Scale of pooled asset base and distribution reach: 13.57 million Assets, 7,747 customer touchpoints and 30 fulfilment centres as of May 31, 2025.
- Customer base of more than 900 customers as of March 31, 2025, including blue-chip companies; the top 10 customers by Fiscal 2025 revenue contribution have each been with the Company for more than five years, and contracts are typically multi-year recurring agreements with select contracts ranging up to five years.
- Comprehensive suite of supply chain assets (pallets, containers and MHE) enabling a larger share of wallet from existing and new customers; the Company has remained PAT positive since 2020.
- Consolidation of industry position through the January 2025 acquisition of CHEP India, which added an established asset pooling network, broadened the customer base and expanded the product portfolio, particularly in containers.
- Technology stack: in-house MyLEAP customer platform, integrated SAP S/4HANA and Salesforce Management enabling electronic data interchange with customers, passive RFID container tracking, IoT/passive RFID in forklifts, and in-house RFID / Asset Audit / Transport Management / POD applications; operations are ISO 27001 certified.
- Product quality and sustainability positioning: FSC-certified spruce-pine-fir pallets, repair and maintenance programmes and quality standards intended to extend asset lifespan, plus internal quality certifications on deployed pallets.
- Promoter and CEO Sunu Mathew has over 26 years of work experience with prior stints at CHEP India Private Limited and L'Oréal India Private Limited; management team spans technology, asset management, finance, procurement and supply chain operations, backed by Corporate Promoter affiliation with KKR.
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Customer contract renewal and top-customer concentration — Customer relationships are typically long-term contractual agreements, with contracts typically multi-year recurring and select contracts ranging up to five years. The DRHP flags that if customers do not renew their agreements or expand the scope of services, or if relationships with top customers are impaired or terminated, business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows could be adversely impacted. The top 10 customers by Fiscal 2025 revenue contribution have each been with the Company for more than five years, concentrating renewal risk in a small set of accounts.
- Capital intensity and rising leverage of the pooled-asset model — The business requires continuous investment in pooled Assets (13.30 million in Fiscal 2025 from 6.93 million in Fiscal 2023). Debt to Equity rose to 0.87 times in Fiscal 2025 from 0.72 times in Fiscal 2024 and 0.62 times in Fiscal 2023. The Fresh Issue of ₹ 4,000.00 million is directed at repayment/prepayment of certain borrowings and general corporate purposes.
- Depreciation-heavy earnings profile — low accounting returns despite high EBITDA margin — Fiscal 2025 EBITDA margin was 56.45% but Return on Equity was only 4.60% and net profit ₹ 375.58 million, against Cash Return on Equity of 23.45% and Cash PAT of ₹ 1,912.87 million. The gap is the depreciation, amortisation and impairment charge on the pooled asset base, which the DRHP itself adds back in defining Cash PAT. Reported PAT is therefore highly sensitive to asset-life and impairment assumptions.
- Acquisition integration and non-comparable / illustrative financials — CHEP India was acquired on January 8, 2025 and merged into the Company, so Fiscal 2025 restated results are not comparable with prior years. The DRHP explicitly warns that the Pro Forma Consolidated Financial Information is presented for illustrative purposes only and may not accurately reflect future financial condition, cash flows and results of operations. The routed extract is also internally inconsistent on the merger effective date (January 2, 2025 in 'Our Business' versus June 2, 2025 in 'Risk Factors' and 'MD&A').
- Dependence on the pace of palletization adoption in a nascent Indian market — Per the F&S Report, India had only 15% palletization in CY2024 against 89% in North America, 91% in the EU, 94% in Australia and New Zealand and 50% in China, and India's pallet industry has only gained momentum and structure over the past 15 years. Growth is contingent on Indian customers converting from fragmented, manual handling to pooled palletized supply chains — a behavioural shift outside the Company's control.
- Utilization-rate sensitivity — Revenue is a function of how much of the owned pool is deployed at customer locations. Container utilization was 76.03% and MHE utilization 81.54% in Fiscal 2025, leaving idle-asset drag; pallet utilization has been effectively flat at 87.46%, 87.75% and 87.85% across Fiscals 2025, 2024 and 2023, so incremental revenue must come from asset additions rather than utilization gains on the pallet pool.
- Promoter and shareholder concentration, with the Offer dominated by an Offer for Sale — Promoters hold 391,393,072 equity shares of face value of ₹1 each, constituting 95.28% of the pre-Offer issued, subscribed and paid-up equity share capital on a fully diluted basis. Of the ₹ 24,000.00 million Offer, ₹ 20,000.00 million is an Offer for Sale (₹ 19,986.23 million by the KKR-affiliated Corporate Promoter Vertical Holdings II Pte. Ltd.) from which the Company receives no proceeds; only ₹ 4,000.00 million is a Fresh Issue.
- Reliance on a commissioned industry report and key-person dependence — The market-leadership and market-size claims throughout the DRHP derive from the F&S Report, which was prepared exclusively for the Offer and commissioned and paid for by the Company for an agreed fee; the DRHP itself carries a dedicated risk factor stating that reliance on such information is subject to inherent risks. Separately, the Individual Promoter Sunu Mathew is simultaneously Chairman, Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, and the DRHP's strengths section leans on his over-26-year career in the pallet industry.

outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: The DRHP describes network and asset-base expansion rather than manufacturing capacity expansion — no plant, line or capex project with a commissioning timeline is disclosed in the routed extract. Growth is presented along three axes. First, inorganic: the Company acquired 100% of the equity capital of CHEP India Private Limited on January 8, 2025 and subsequently merged it into the Company, adding CHEP India's established pallet and container pooling network (F&S recognised CHEP India as market leader in asset pooling in the container segment in Fiscal 2024), thereby expanding reach across industries, broadening the customer base and enlarging the product portfolio, particularly in containers. Second, organic asset build: total Assets rose to 13.30 million in Fiscal 2025 from 7.92 million in Fiscal 2024 and 6.93 million in Fiscal 2023, reaching 13.57 million as of May 31, 2025, supported by a pan-India footprint of 7,747 customer touchpoints and 30 fulfilment centres. Third, market headroom: per the F&S Report, India had only 15% palletization in CY2024 against 89% in North America, 91% in the EU, 94% in Australia and New Zealand and 50% in China, with North America running a 1,092 million-unit pallet pooling market (55% penetration of total pallet circulation) and the EU 1,500 million pooled units (45% penetration) — India's pallet industry is described as relatively young, having gained momentum and structure over the past 15 years. The Fresh Issue proceeds are earmarked for debt repayment and general corporate purposes, not for a named expansion project.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Revenue mix shift toward MHE pooling: in Fiscal 2025 Total Income split was Asset Pooling excluding MHE ₹ 3,842.20 million, MHE Pooling ₹ 886.74 million and Others ₹ 121.37 million; MHE pooling scaled from ₹ 75.72 million in Fiscal 2023 to ₹ 675.83 million in Fiscal 2024 to ₹ 886.74 million in Fiscal 2025, making it the fastest-growing line.
- Utilization rate is the core operating lever: Fiscal 2025 pallet utilization 87.46% (87.75% Fiscal 2024, 87.85% Fiscal 2023), container utilization 76.03% (66.17% Fiscal 2024, 39.68% Fiscal 2023) and MHE utilization 81.54% (82.50% Fiscal 2024, N.A. Fiscal 2023). Container utilization improvement is the clearest mix/efficiency gain; pallet utilization has been broadly flat.
- Asset-base scale-up drives revenue: total Assets 13.30 million in Fiscal 2025 versus 7.92 million in Fiscal 2024 and 6.93 million in Fiscal 2023.
- Margin structure: EBITDA margin 56.45% in Fiscal 2025, 56.44% in Fiscal 2024 and 48.92% in Fiscal 2023 — a step-up between Fiscal 2023 and Fiscal 2024 that has since held flat. Cash PAT Margin was 39.44% in Fiscal 2025 versus 40.27% in Fiscal 2024 and 32.17% in Fiscal 2023.
- Depreciation intensity separates accounting from cash returns: the DRHP defines Cash PAT as net profit plus depreciation, amortisation and impairment expenses. In Fiscal 2025 Return on Equity was 4.60% against Cash Return on Equity of 23.45% (Fiscal 2024: 5.79% versus 23.34%; Fiscal 2023: 1.67% versus 15.38%), and Return on Capital Employed (by EBITDA) was 18.01% versus 20.33% in Fiscal 2024.
- Rising leverage funding the asset build: Debt to Equity was 0.87 times in Fiscal 2025 versus 0.72 times in Fiscal 2024 and 0.62 times in Fiscal 2023.
- Contract economics: customer relationships are typically long-term, multi-year recurring contracts with select contracts ranging up to five years, and the DRHP states that the margins earned from these long-term contracts are dependent on pricing, volume and operational efficiencies.
- Comparability break from the CHEP India acquisition: because CHEP India was acquired on January 8, 2025 and merged into the Company, the Restated Consolidated Financial Information for Fiscal 2025 is not comparable to prior years, and the DRHP separately presents Pro Forma Consolidated Financial Information for the year ended March 31, 2025 as if the acquisition had been completed on April 1, 2024.

risks.note: Customer relationships are typically long-term contractual agreements, with contracts typically multi-year recurring and select contracts ranging up to five years. The DRHP flags that if customers do not renew their agreements or expand the scope of services, or if relationships with top customers are impaired or terminated, business, financial condition, results of operations and cash flows could be adversely impacted. The top 10 customers by Fiscal 2025 revenue contribution have each been with the Company for more than five years, concentrating renewal risk in a small set of accounts.
risks.risk: Customer contract renewal and top-customer concentration

risks.note: The business requires continuous investment in pooled Assets (13.30 million in Fiscal 2025 from 6.93 million in Fiscal 2023). Debt to Equity rose to 0.87 times in Fiscal 2025 from 0.72 times in Fiscal 2024 and 0.62 times in Fiscal 2023. The Fresh Issue of ₹ 4,000.00 million is directed at repayment/prepayment of certain borrowings and general corporate purposes.
risks.risk: Capital intensity and rising leverage of the pooled-asset model

risks.note: Fiscal 2025 EBITDA margin was 56.45% but Return on Equity was only 4.60% and net profit ₹ 375.58 million, against Cash Return on Equity of 23.45% and Cash PAT of ₹ 1,912.87 million. The gap is the depreciation, amortisation and impairment charge on the pooled asset base, which the DRHP itself adds back in defining Cash PAT. Reported PAT is therefore highly sensitive to asset-life and impairment assumptions.
risks.risk: Depreciation-heavy earnings profile — low accounting returns despite high EBITDA margin

risks.note: CHEP India was acquired on January 8, 2025 and merged into the Company, so Fiscal 2025 restated results are not comparable with prior years. The DRHP explicitly warns that the Pro Forma Consolidated Financial Information is presented for illustrative purposes only and may not accurately reflect future financial condition, cash flows and results of operations. risks.note: Per the F&S Report, India had only 15% palletization in CY2024 against 89% in North America, 91% in the EU, 94% in Australia and New Zealand and 50% in China, and India's pallet industry has only gained momentum and structure over the past 15 years. Growth is contingent on Indian customers converting from fragmented, manual handling to pooled palletized supply chains — a behavioural shift outside the Company's control.
risks.risk: Dependence on the pace of palletization adoption in a nascent Indian market

risks.note: Revenue is a function of how much of the owned pool is deployed at customer locations. Container utilization was 76.03% and MHE utilization 81.54% in Fiscal 2025, leaving idle-asset drag; pallet utilization has been effectively flat at 87.46%, 87.75% and 87.85% across Fiscals 2025, 2024 and 2023, so incremental revenue must come from asset additions rather than utilization gains on the pallet pool.

business_ops.seasonality: The business is dependent on the operational scale and financial health of customers. Fluctuations in customers' production volumes, driven by macroeconomic conditions, seasonal demand, or changes in their own business strategies, directly affect demand for the Company's asset pooling services. During periods of increased manufacturing activity, the Company may experience higher utilization rates and revenue growth; conversely, during downturns or periods of reduced output, its services may be underutilized, leading to lower revenues and potential inefficiencies in asset deployment. This dependency on customers' business cycles introduces a level of unpredictability to financial performance and operational planning. No quantified seasonality of the Company's own revenue is disclosed in this text.
business_ops.supply_chain_integration: The Company operates a 'share and reuse' (pooling) model under which ownership and management of the Assets sits with the Company and is provided to customers as a service, enabling customers to operate an asset-light model by hiring and de-hiring Assets. According to the F&S Report, the Company operates a full-service model covering warehousing and distribution of returnable packaging Assets. Upstream, pallets are made with 100% SPF sourced from certified, sustainable international suppliers from Europe and Oceanic countries, and FSC certified SPF is used; the top ten suppliers and service providers contributed 60.00% of total purchases in Fiscal 2025. Downstream, as of May 31, 2025 the Company has 13.57 million Assets and maintains a pan-India network of 7,747 customer touchpoints and 30 fulfilment centres, which facilitate storage, maintenance, repair and rapid deployment of Assets; the extensive pan-India network enables the Company to leverage reverse logistics for pallet retrieval at a competitive cost. Maintenance and repairs are handled by the Company's own quality and repairs team, on-site or offsite as applicable, and repair and maintenance programs are run to extend asset lifespan. Technology is in-house and integrated: the in-house developed MyLEAP platform provides customers an interface for order tracking and management, recent order details, swapping damaged Assets, reports and support; SAP S/4HANA and Salesforce Management are integrated to enable electronic data interchange with customers; passive RFID technology is used to monitor containers through the supply chain; and IoT or passive RFID solutions are implemented in forklifts to track forklift movements at customer locations. In-house mobile and web applications include the RFID App, Asset Audit App, Transport Management System and Proof of Delivery (POD) App. The Company consolidated its position by acquiring 100% of the equity capital of CHEP India Private Limited on January 8, 2025, integrating CHEP India's established asset pooling network with its own and increasing its product portfolio, in particular in relation to the container business; TARON is the Company's subsidiary in forklift pooling. Product breadth spans pallets, containers and MHEs, allowing customers to deal with one partner rather than coordinating with multiple suppliers.

overview.business_model: The Company pools supply chain assets rather than selling them: it offers pallets (flat carrier structures that support goods in a stable manner while being handled by forklifts, pallet jacks or conveyors), containers and material handling equipment (equipment used in managing a warehouse) to customers on a share-and-reuse basis. Customer relationships are typically characterised by long-term contractual agreements, with contracts typically being multi-year recurring contracts and select contracts ranging up to five years; margins earned from these long-term contracts are dependent on pricing, volume and operational efficiencies. A portion of revenue is derived from the hiring and de-hiring of Assets that are individually customised to customers' specifications, and the Company is also responsible for providing equipment repair and maintenance services to customers, on or offsite, as applicable. Total revenue from operations was Rs 4,664.72 million in Fiscal 2025, Rs 3,649.71 million in Fiscal 2024 and Rs 2,533.67 million in Fiscal 2023 (Rs 6,210.22 million for Fiscal 2025 on a pro forma basis including contribution from customers of CHEP India).

compliance_legal.detail: The Competition Act, 2002 prohibits agreements causing an appreciable adverse effect on competition (AAEC) in India, which are void and result in imposition of substantial monetary penalties, and prohibits abuse of a dominant position. Where a contravention took place with the consent, connivance or attributable neglect of any director, manager, secretary or other officer, that person may also be guilty and punished. Combination provisions require acquisitions of shares, voting rights, assets or control, or mergers or amalgamations crossing prescribed asset and turnover thresholds, to be mandatorily notified to and pre-approved by the CCI. The CCI has extra-territorial powers over agreements, abusive conduct or combinations occurring outside India having an AAEC in India.

compliance_legal.title: Risk Factor 54 — Adverse application or interpretation of competition laws in India

compliance_legal.detail: The Company is incorporated under the laws of India, all Directors, Key Managerial Personnel and members of Senior Management are residents of India and all assets are located in India, so it may not be possible to effect service of process outside India or enforce foreign judgments predicated upon civil liabilities under laws other than Indian law. Recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments is provided for under Section 13 and Section 44A of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. India is not party to any international treaty on recognition or enforcement of foreign judgments and has reciprocal arrangements with only a limited number of jurisdictions. Judgments from non-reciprocating territories, such as the United States, cannot be enforced through execution proceedings and require instituting a fresh suit in India. A party seeking to enforce a foreign judgment in India requires prior RBI approval to repatriate any amount recovered.
compliance_legal.evidence: Reciprocating jurisdictions named: the United Kingdom, Hong Kong, Republic of Singapore, United Arab Emirates, among others. 'The party in whose favor such final foreign judgment is rendered may initiate a fresh suit in a competent court in India within three years of obtaining such final foreign judgment. Generally, there are considerable delays in the disposal of suits by Indian courts.'
compliance_legal.title: Risk Factor 57 — Difficulty enforcing foreign judgments in India against the Company or its management

compliance_legal.detail: Under the Companies Act, an Indian company having share capital must offer its equity shareholders pre-emptive rights to subscribe and pay for a proportionate number of equity shares to maintain existing ownership percentages prior to issuance of new equity shares, unless waived by special resolution. If the law of the investor's jurisdiction does not permit exercise of such pre-emptive rights without the Company filing an offering document or registration statement, the investor will be unable to exercise them unless such filing is made. If the Company elects not to file a registration statement, new securities may be issued to a custodian who may sell them for the benefit of investors, and the value received on such sale and related transaction costs cannot be predicted.
compliance_legal.evidence: Waiver requires 'adoption of a special resolution by holders of three-fourths of the equity shares voting on such resolution'.
compliance_legal.title: Risk Factor 61 — Restrictions on holders' ability to exercise pre-emptive rights under Indian law

compliance_legal.detail: Under current Indian tax laws, unless specifically exempted, capital gains arising from the sale of equity shares of an Indian company are generally taxable in India, and a securities transaction tax is levied on equity shares sold on an Indian stock exchange. Capital gains arising from sale of the Equity Shares will not be chargeable to tax in India where relief is provided under a treaty read with the Multilateral Instrument, and the Company may or may not grant the benefit of a tax treaty to a non-resident shareholder for the purposes of deducting tax at source. Residents of other countries may be liable for tax in India as well as in their own jurisdictions. Liability to pay stamp duty on sale of securities through stock exchanges rests on the buyer absent a specific agreement provision, and on the transferor in other cases of transfer for consideration through a depository.
compliance_legal.evidence: 'Any capital gains exceeding ₹125,000, realized on the sale of listed equity shares on a recognised stock exchange, held for more than 12 months may be subject to long-term capital gains tax in India at the rate of 12.5% (plus applicable surcharge and cess).' Listed equity shares held more than 12 months sold off a recognised stock exchange with no STT paid: long term capital gains tax at 10% (plus applicable surcharge and cess), without indexation benefits. Held 12 months or less: short term capital gains tax at 20% (plus applicable surcharge and cess), subject to STT being paid. Stamp duty for transfer of securities other than debentures: 0.015% on a delivery basis and 0.003% on a non-delivery basis of the consideration amount. Finance (No.2) Act of 2024, notified August 16, 2024: increase in the deduction available in respect of private sector employer's contribution to National Pension Scheme from 10% to 14% of salary.
compliance_legal.title: Risk Factor 66 — Indian taxes on income arising on the sale of Equity Shares and on dividends received

Global conflicts, sanctions, failure or abandonment of free trade agreements, introduction of duties and taxes on imported goods and other trade barriers may impede cross-border trade, production and demand. The global credit and equity markets have from time to time experienced substantial dislocations, liquidity disruptions and market corrections, and policy measures may not have the intended stabilising effects.
financial_valuation.evidence: Conflicts cited between Israel and Palestine and between Russia and Ukraine; sanctions imposed by governments in the United States, United Kingdom and European Union on certain products, industry sectors and parties in Russia. 'China is one of India's major trading partners and there are rising concerns of a possible slowdown in the Chinese economy as well as a strained relationship with India.'
financial_valuation.title: Risk Factor 55 — Financial instability in other countries may cause increased volatility in Indian financial markets

Adverse revisions by international rating agencies may adversely affect the Company's ratings, the terms on which it can raise additional finance or refinance existing indebtedness (including overseas), and the interest rates and other commercial terms at which such financing is available.
financial_valuation.evidence: No quantified figures disclosed in this risk factor.

internal_operational.detail: Customer relationships are typically multi-year recurring contracts with select contracts ranging up to five years. Non-renewal, failure to expand scope, failure to meet specified quality standards (which may permit termination), inability to fulfil immediate demand for Assets, customer pricing leverage, customer production-volume cycles and customer insolvency are all cited as capable of reducing revenue and utilisation. A portion of revenue derives from hiring/de-hiring of Assets customised to individual customer specifications which cannot readily be repurposed, creating inventory-obsolescence risk. The DRHP states it had no instances of exiting customer contracts with material impact in Fiscals 2025, 2024 and 2023.
internal_operational.evidence: Revenue contribution — Top 10 customers: ₹1,783.27 million / 28.72% (Fiscal 2025 pro forma), ₹1,594.56 million / 34.18% (Fiscal 2025), ₹1,441.30 million / 39.49% (Fiscal 2024), ₹957.01 million / 37.77% (Fiscal 2023). Top 11 to top 50: ₹1,749.36 million / 28.17%, ₹1,334.73 million / 28.61%, ₹1,047.80 million / 28.71%, ₹800.44 million / 31.59%. Top 51 to top 100: ₹876.26 million / 14.11%, ₹661.90 million / 14.19%, ₹531.53 million / 14.56%, ₹378.61 million / 14.94%. Others: ₹1,801.33 million / 29.00%, ₹1,073.53 million / 23.02%, ₹629.08 million / 17.24%, ₹397.61 million / 15.69%. Total revenue from operations: ₹6,210.22 million (Fiscal 2025 pro forma), ₹4,664.72 million (Fiscal 2025), ₹3,649.71 million (Fiscal 2024), ₹2,533.67 million (Fiscal 2023). Contracts 'ranging up to five years'. One customer declared bankrupt in January 2023 requiring retrieval of Assets; 'we did not face any material losses'.
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 1 — Long-term recurring customer contracts; non-renewal or loss of top customers

internal_operational.detail: Operations depend on in-house and third-party IT systems and software, including for billing. Systems are stated to be vulnerable to defects, system failures, unexpected high transaction volume, cyberattacks, human error, natural disasters, power loss, viruses, ransomware and malware. Malfunction of IT systems, including data-storage infrastructure, could generate inaccurate, incomplete, duplicate or erroneous invoices. The Company also integrates its systems with customers' IT systems and may fail to do so successfully.
internal_operational.evidence: Disclosed incidents: shutdown of power supply in the server room in January 2025; compromise of the password for the marketing department email account in March 2024; firewall system became unresponsive due to suspicious traffic in November 2024; anonymous system attack on 'TARON' domain emails in May 2025. The DRHP states none of these incidents had a material financial impact/material impact on operations.
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 2 — Reliance on technology infrastructure; disruption, cyber-security and billing-integrity risk

internal_operational.detail: The business relies on continuous ownership and management of pooling equipment (pallets, crates) as Assets move through the supply chain. Loss or leakage is described as an inherent risk; if the rate of asset loss exceeds commercially acceptable thresholds the Company must write off lost Assets and incur replacement costs. Contracts include provisions to recover cost of lost Assets from customers, but customers may not pay. Assets are tracked using passive RFID tags and IoT solutions; excessively damaged Assets must be scrapped.
internal_operational.evidence: Impairment loss due to Assets lost and not yet recovered from customers: ₹52.39 million (Fiscal 2025), ₹53.52 million (Fiscal 2024), ₹3.07 million (Fiscal 2023). Net block (net book value of property, plant and equipment): ₹12,293.40 million, ₹9,750.25 million, ₹8,058.04 million. Loss as % of net block: 0.43%, 0.55%, 0.04%.
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 3 — Pooling asset loss/leakage and inadequate controls on pooling equipment

internal_operational.detail: Success is linked to consistently delivering reliable, quality and uniform services; customers expect adherence to stringent quality standards for operations and equipment. Failure could result in negative customer perception, reduced usage, claims by customers, penalties, damages, product recall or redesign. Increasing automation in manufacturing plants and distribution centres often requires pallets and equipment meeting higher quality specifications or entirely new equipment, and greater customer emphasis on pallet safety may require further investment in higher-quality or safer equipment, potentially increasing operational costs.
internal_operational.evidence: Sourcing standards, testing protocols and certifications from recognized bodies such as the Indian Institute of Packaging ('IIP'); timber sourced from certified international suppliers. 'While we have not faced any such instances in Fiscals 2025, 2024 and 2023 which resulted in our incurring significant costs.'
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 5 — Failure to set and/or meet quality standards in relation to Assets

internal_operational.detail: The Company is responsible for inspecting, cleaning and repairing pooled Assets before reissue; Assets unsuitable for repair must be scrapped. It has limited control over end-use of pooled Assets, so an increase in the number of pallets or containers requiring repair, or in the extent and frequency of repairs, would escalate inspection and repair costs. Maintenance costs are stated to be influenced by cost of labour or materials including timber, customer handling practices, type of goods transported, return rate and cycle time.
internal_operational.evidence: Repairs and maintenance expensed in the restated consolidated statement of profit and loss: ₹267.11 million (Fiscal 2025), ₹295.02 million (Fiscal 2024), ₹356.20 million (Fiscal 2023).
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 6 — Increases in maintenance may result in additional expenses

internal_operational.detail: The Company depends on suppliers and service providers for purchase of Assets and ancillary services such as transportation. Although Assets are typically procured from more than one supplier, there is no assurance this can continue or that alternative suppliers of the same quality can be located if arrangements terminate. The Company may be unable to pass all cost increases on to customers, and may be required to replace a supplier if Assets do not meet safety, compliance, quality or performance standards or if a supplier suspends or discontinues operations.
internal_operational.evidence: Base of 381 suppliers as of March 31, 2025. Top ten suppliers' contribution to total purchases: ₹2,630.21 million / 60.00% (Fiscal 2025), ₹2,705.92 million / 77.00% (Fiscal 2024), ₹1,903.26 million / 75.11% (Fiscal 2023). Fiscal 2025 named/largest: Supplier 1^ ₹808.92 million / 18.45%; SNG Timbers Private Limited ₹513.36 million / 11.71%; Shree Shipping Services Private Limited ₹284.19 million / 6.48%; Supplier 4^ ₹250.80 million / 5.72%; Supplier 5^ ₹169.16 million / 3.86%; Supplier 6^ ₹156.60 million / 3.57%; Supplier 7^ ₹122.65 million / 2.80%; Shanadzzar Logistics (India) Private Limited ₹110.11 million / 2.51%; Prozo Integrated Logistics Private Limited ₹109.66 million / 2.50%; Supplier 10^ ₹104.76 million / 2.39%. Fiscal 2024: Supplier 1^ ₹867.01 million / 24.67%; SNG Timbers ₹390.76 million / 11.12%; Supplier 3^ ₹364.05 million / 10.36%. Fiscal 2023: Supplier 1^ ₹487.21 million / 19.23%; Supplier 2^ ₹445.62 million / 17.59%; SNG Timbers ₹228.20 million / 9.01%. '^The names of certain of our top 10 suppliers have not been disclosed in this Draft Red Herring Prospectus due to non-receipt of consent from these suppliers.'
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 10 — Dependence on suppliers and service providers; top ten suppliers concentration

internal_operational.detail: Operations are exposed to volatility in the supply and pricing of timber and plastic, the critical raw materials for pallets and containers respectively. The Company does not directly source timber or plastic; its pallet and container suppliers procure the raw materials, with the Company providing quality benchmarks and guidelines. Climate and nature related risks for forests and timber supply (market, regulatory and physical) may emerge. Forklifts are procured from China, exposing the Company to geopolitical, regulatory, logistical, economic and operational uncertainty including import restrictions, enhanced customs scrutiny, higher duties, non-tariff barriers and delays in import licences. Depreciation of the Indian Rupee against the currencies in which raw materials and certain Assets are sourced increases Rupee-equivalent import costs and compresses gross margins.
internal_operational.evidence: Suppliers primarily source timber from Europe and Oceanic countries. Timber prices increased due to the COVID-19 pandemic in Fiscal 2020 and disruptions in global trade routes, including those related to the Red Sea in Fiscal 2024. Forklifts procured from China.
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 11 — Volatility in supply and pricing of raw materials (timber, plastic), imported forklifts and foreign currency

internal_operational.detail: Operations are subject to accidents at work, fire, earthquakes, floods, force majeure events, acts of terrorism and explosions, including hazards that may destroy inventory. Policies maintained include contractors plant and machinery, fire, storm, burglary, terrorism, riots/strikes and malicious damage, marine import and transit of raw material and goods insurance, and directors' & officers' liability insurance. Future claims may be rejected in full or in part, and losses exceeding aggregate coverage limits would be borne by the Company. Insurance coverage expires from time to time and is renewed in the ordinary course.
internal_operational.evidence: Insurance cover (A): ₹17,507.63 million (Fiscal 2025), ₹14,242.55 million (Fiscal 2024), ₹11,761.96 million (Fiscal 2023). Total assets (B): ₹12,295.25 million, ₹9,764.85 million, ₹8,058.53 million. Insurance coverage ratio (C = A/B): 142.39%, 145.86%, 145.96%. 'Our insurance claims have not exceeded our insurance coverage and we have not recognized any losses in Fiscals 2025, 2024 and 2023 due to the partial or full rejection of our claims by our insurers.'
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 16 — Insurance coverage may not be sufficient or adequately protect against risks

internal_operational.detail: The Company is dependent on reliable supply of pallets from third-party manufacturers and suppliers and depends on a limited number of suppliers for pallets. Significant increases in pallet cost (from raw material prices, supply chain disruptions or inflation) could adversely affect operating results; because agreements are typically long term up to five years, increased costs may not be passed on in a timely manner or at all. Shortfalls may arise from supply chain bottlenecks, labour shortages or increased competition for limited pallet supplies.
internal_operational.evidence: Costs incurred towards additions in pallets: ₹2,017.00 million / 43.24% of total revenue from operations (Fiscal 2025), ₹1,869.22 million / 51.22% (Fiscal 2024), ₹1,171.82 million / 46.25% (Fiscal 2023). Timber price increases cited from the COVID-19 pandemic in Fiscal 2020 and Red Sea trade-route disruptions in Fiscal 2024. Agreements 'typically ... long term agreements up to five years'.
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 18 — Volatility in supply and pricing of pallets required for the pallet pooling business

internal_operational.detail: The Company must attract, train, motivate and retain experienced professionals and highly skilled employees, and depends on uninterrupted availability of trained and safety-conscious MHE operators including forklift drivers. Elevated attrition of contract labour such as MHE operators obliges recurring hiring costs, training expenses, sign-on incentives and wage escalations, and heightens risk of operational disruptions, scheduling inefficiencies and safety incidents from insufficiently experienced replacement staff.
internal_operational.evidence: Total number of KMPs: 3 / 3 / 3 (Fiscals 2025 / 2024 / 2023); attrition rate of KMPs: 67.00% / 67.00% / 33.00%. Members of Senior Management (other than KMPs): 6 / 6 / 5; attrition rate: 33.00% / 33.00% / 20.00%. Permanent employees: 364 / 268 / 269; attrition rate: 36.81% / 48.13% / 40.52%. MHE operators: 1,665 / 1,315 / 1,015; attrition rate: 47.00% / 65.00% / 77.00%. Attrition rate is stated to be voluntary resignations divided by headcount at the beginning of the period plus additions during the period, excluding superannuation and involuntary resignations.
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 20 — Dependence on KMPs, Senior Management and other employees; attrition including MHE operators

internal_operational.detail: Independent contractors are appointed who in turn engage onsite contract workers for certain operations including at fulfilment centres and customer touchpoints. Although contract workers are not engaged directly, the Company is responsible for wage payments in the event of default by the independent contractors. The business is labour intensive, with risks relating to cost, availability and skill of contract workers, including during peak, festive or harvesting periods.
internal_operational.evidence: Number of contract workers: 337 (Fiscal 2025), 158 (Fiscal 2024), 264 (Fiscal 2023). Expenses towards contract workers: ₹155.17 million, ₹115.86 million, ₹118.19 million; 3.58%, 3.56%, 4.76% of total expenses. 'None of our employees were associated with any labor union as of March 31, 2025.'
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 25 — Non-availability of contract workers at reasonable cost; strikes, work stoppages or wage demands

internal_operational.detail: Pooled pallets and containers present a contamination risk within the supply chain. Wooden pallets, being porous, can absorb moisture and are prone to harbouring bacteria, mould, pests or chemical residues; the pooling model heightens this as shared pallets may transfer contaminants or pests between customers or facilities, potentially leading to regulatory violations and reputational harm, particularly for food, pharmaceutical or other sensitive products. Pallets are inspected at de-hire and contaminated pallets are quarantined and scrapped; contaminated containers may be rendered unusable and scrapped, increasing inventory write-offs, waste-handling expenses and new container purchase costs.
internal_operational.evidence: 'We had an incident in April 2025 where an oil spill resulted in the contamination of certain of our pallets. While we were able to recover the associated costs due to contamination from our customers, there is no assurance that such an incident will not occur in the future.'
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 27 — Contamination of pallets and containers

internal_operational.detail: The Company provides material handling equipment (MHE) such as forklifts, pallet jacks and other machinery to customers. Accidents or equipment failures can cause property damage, personal injury or fatalities at customer sites, arising from equipment malfunction, improper handling by MHE operators, operating without following safety protocols, improper use by customers, inadequate maintenance or unforeseen mechanical defects. The Company may face third-party liability claims, medical costs and reimbursements, legal proceedings, regulatory investigations or enforcement actions.
internal_operational.evidence: 'While we have not faced any such instances in Fiscal 2025, 2024 and 2023, there is no assurance that we will not face such instances in the future.'
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 28 — Risks related to the provision and use of MHEs

internal_operational.detail: As on the date of the DRHP, fulfilment centres and offices, including the Registered and Corporate Office, are situated in buildings or on land leased/licensed from third parties and are not owned. Termination or failure to renew on favourable terms could require vacating premises. Regulatory non-compliance by landlords or adverse developments in landlords' title or ownership rights may disrupt operations. Deeds for existing and future leased properties may not be adequately stamped and/or registered, and stamp duty paid may not be accepted as evidence in a court of law, with penalties possible for inadequate stamp duty.
internal_operational.evidence: Lease tenures of fulfilment centres range from 9 months to 5 years. Expenses incurred towards lease rentals (including undiscounted lease payments): ₹447.32 million (Fiscal 2025), ₹306.18 million (Fiscal 2024), ₹234.71 million (Fiscal 2023).
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 29 — Fulfilment centres and offices situated on leased premises

internal_operational.detail: The Company is described as deeply reliant on natural resources, particularly forestry products, for the timber required in manufacturing and repair of pallets, and its operations both depend on and impact nature and biodiversity in its regions and broader supply chain including forests. Growing societal and customer awareness creates increasing scrutiny and exposure to physical risks (acute or chronic effects of ecosystem degradation), transitional risks (evolving policies, legal requirements, technological changes, market expectations, reputational considerations) and systemic risks.
internal_operational.evidence: 'While we have not had any instances where the failure to effectively manage our relationship with natural capital and biodiversity led to additional costs, loss of income and reputational damage, there is no assurance that we will be able to continue to do that.'
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 30 — Increased societal and customer focus on natural capital and biodiversity issues

internal_operational.detail: Severe flooding, lightning strikes, earthquakes, extreme wind conditions, severe storms, wildfires and other unfavourable weather conditions (including those from climate change) or natural disasters could damage warehouses, offices or other assets or require shutdown of operations, impeding on-boarding of new customers or collection of payments. Catastrophic events such as explosions, terrorist acts or riots could result in personal injury, loss of life, environmental danger or severe damage to or destruction of offices or field activities.
internal_operational.evidence: 'Certain of our customer touchpoints have suffered natural disasters in recent years including floods, while the damage caused by such natural disasters have been covered pursuant to insurance claims, there is no assurance that our we will be able to continue to do so.'
internal_operational.title: Risk Factor 52 — Natural or man-made disasters in the locations of operation

strategy_growth.detail: A significant portion of revenues is derived from the pallet pooling business (sale of services – pallets). Adverse developments affecting the pallet pooling market, including increased competition, changes in customer preferences, regulatory shifts or technological disruptions, could impact the business; loss of revenue from a key customer reducing reliance on pooled pallets, switching to alternative solutions or negotiating less favourable terms may not be offset by gains in other business segments. The Company primarily offers wooden pallets on a pooling basis; a shift in market preference toward plastic or metal pallets, or loss of popularity of the pooling model in favour of one-way pallets, could cause loss of market share, additional capital expenditure to diversify pallet offerings, operational challenges in adapting infrastructure, potential obsolescence of wooden pallet inventory, and underutilisation of existing Assets.
strategy_growth.evidence: Revenue from operations – pallet pooling: ₹3,906.13 million / 62.90% of total revenue from operations (Fiscal 2025 pro forma), ₹3,167.44 million / 67.90% (Fiscal 2025), ₹2,636.17 million / 72.23% (Fiscal 2024), ₹2,131.93 million / 84.14% (Fiscal 2023).
strategy_growth.title: Risk Factor 7 — Majority of revenue from operations derived from the pallet pooling business

strategy_growth.detail: Competition in the global pallet pooling market is defined by the scale, network efficiency and sustainability credentials of a few dominant players. While the Company currently faces limited competition, new competitors may enter the market and may possess greater financial resources or the ability to invest heavily in advertising and marketing. A new entrant introducing an alternative supply chain methodology, for instance one-way pallets, could reduce demand for pooled pallets. Increased competition may be based on pricing, innovation, brand recognition, promotional activities and introduction of new services.
strategy_growth.evidence: 'Globally, this industry is typically characterized as a monopoly or duopoly within individual countries. The Indian pallet pooling industry exhibits high barriers to entry, limiting competition and allowing a select few players to dominate across geographies. (Source: F&S Report)'
strategy_growth.title: Risk Factor 8 — Competition in the industry could reduce market share

strategy_growth.detail: The Company has expanded its operations and experienced growth and profitability over the last few years, but there is no assurance the growth strategy will continue to be successful or that it will be able to continue to grow or enhance profitability, or at the same rate. Historical growth rates and profitability may not be indicative of future growth and profitability, and there is no assurance of maintaining past growth rate, profitability or securing the same number of customers. The Company may from time to time look for opportunities to acquire businesses or enter strategic partnerships or alliances, which could disrupt ongoing business, distract management and employees and increase expenses.
strategy_growth.evidence: Revenue from operations: ₹4,664.72 million (Fiscal 2025), ₹3,649.71 million (Fiscal 2024), ₹2,533.67 million (Fiscal 2023); year-on-year growth 27.81%, 44.05%, 19.88%. Total income: ₹4,850.31 million, ₹3,719.44 million, ₹2,581.65 million. Net profit for the year: ₹357.58 million, ₹371.74 million, ₹90.11 million (as printed in this Risk Factor 17 table). EBITDA: ₹2,737.97 million, ₹2,099.18 million, ₹1,262.92 million; EBITDA margin 56.45%, 56.44%, 48.92%. Note to table: 'The pro forma revenue from operations for Fiscal 2025 was ₹6,210.22 million, total income was ₹6,858.91 million, profit before tax was ₹679.78 million, net profit for the year was ₹482.51 million, EBITDA was ₹3,247.97 and EBITDA margin was 47.35%.' (The MD&A Non-GAAP reconciliation elsewhere in this text prints net profit for the year Fiscal 2025 as ₹375.58 million.)
strategy_growth.title: Risk Factor 17 — Rapid recent growth may not be sustainable, and profitability may not be maintained

strategy_growth.detail: The emergence of new technologies in pallet, container or MHE design or components could pose a threat to competitive position; more cost-effective or efficient alternatives may draw customers and other supply chain participants away. Introduction of alternative technologies could prompt customers to restructure their supply chains, adopt different logistics models, or implement alternative asset management strategies that reduce or eliminate the need for pooling services. Shifts in supply chain practices such as increased automation and adoption of reusable packaging systems could further diminish the relevance of the Company's Assets. Remaining competitive might compel significant investments in new technologies or adaptation of the business model.
strategy_growth.evidence: Expenses on technology (comprising expenses on software and information technology per the Restated Consolidated Financial Information): ₹27.86 million (Fiscal 2025), ₹18.27 million (Fiscal 2024), ₹13.59 million (Fiscal 2023); as a % of total expenses: 0.64%, 0.56%, 0.55%.
strategy_growth.title: Risk Factor 21 — New technologies in pallet, container or MHE design or components may reduce competitiveness

strategy_growth.detail: The Company may rely on strategic acquisitions and similar investments for access to new geographies or product line expansion, and may enter strategic partnerships. Timely receipt of requisite permits, licences or approvals is critical; government authorities could delay or block acquisitions on antitrust grounds, and disputes may arise. The Company may experience difficulties integrating acquisitions, including differing operations, technologies and corporate cultures, unexpected costs and operational disruptions, and risk of absorbing unforeseen liabilities or compliance issues not fully identified during due diligence. Future acquisitions may expose it to integration risks for new operations, services and personnel, hidden liabilities, diversion of resources, inability to generate sufficient revenue to offset acquisition costs, and potential loss of or harm to relationships with employees, suppliers or customers.
strategy_growth.evidence: 'On January 8, 2025, we acquired CHEP India Private Limited and pursuant to order dated April 17, 2025, from the National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai, CHEP India (our erstwhile wholly owned subsidiary) was merged with our Company with effect from June 2, 2025.' 'In February 2023, we acquired Skan Marine Services Private Limited and pursuant to order dated May 29, 2024, from the National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai, Skan (our erstwhile subsidiary) was merged with our Company with effect from June 21, 2024.'
strategy_growth.title: Risk Factor 26 — Inorganic growth and integration of acquired businesses may not yield timely or effective results

strategy_growth.detail: Brand and reputation are described as among the Company's most important assets, developed through focused and consistent branding and marketing initiatives to grow sales, revenues and market share and expand into new markets. Any adverse publicity involving the Company or any of its products, even if factually incorrect, may impair reputation, dilute the impact of branding and marketing initiatives, and may be accelerated through the internet given increased use of social media in India. Adverse publicity about regulatory or legal action could damage reputation and brand image and reduce long-term demand even if unfounded or immaterial to operations.
strategy_growth.evidence: Brands 'LEAP' and 'TARON'. Marketing expenses: ₹21.85 million (Fiscal 2025), ₹25.41 million (Fiscal 2024), ₹23.40 million (Fiscal 2023); marketing expenses as a % of total expenses: 0.50%, 0.78%, 0.94%.
strategy_growth.title: Risk Factor 33 — Inability to maintain, protect and grow brand image

strategy_growth.detail: The Company is dependent on prevailing economic conditions in India and its results are affected by factors influencing the Indian economy and the regional markets in which it operates, including the macroeconomic climate (increases in Indian interest rates or inflation), scarcity of credit or other financing, volatility in trading activity on India's principal stock exchanges, changes in India's tax, trade, fiscal or monetary policies, political instability, terrorism or military conflict, deterioration in relations between India and its neighbouring countries, and any downgrading of India's debt rating. Global developments including conflicts and sanctions can significantly impact India, and a trade war between large economies may increase risk aversion and volatility in global capital markets.
strategy_growth.evidence: Events cited: 'the recent attack in Pahalgam, Jammu and Kashmir in April 2025'; the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, and Israel and Iran; sanctions imposed by Governments in the United States, United Kingdom and the European Union on certain products, industry sectors and parties in Russia; geopolitical tensions arising from Israel and Hamas; 'the potential expulsion of migrant workers in the US'.
strategy_growth.title: Risk Factor 47 — Adverse development or slowdown in the Indian economy, political or other factors beyond control

strategy_growth.detail: The business may be exposed to international trade policies, geopolitical tensions and the imposition of tariffs, export controls or economic sanctions, which are inherently unpredictable and beyond the Company's control. Geopolitical tensions and economic sanctions may lead to restrictions on material procurement in certain countries.
strategy_growth.evidence: 'In 2025, US President Donald Trump implemented tariffs on several major trading partners, including India, Canada and the European Union. These tariffs together with countermeasures that have been or may be adopted by trading partners affected by these tariffs are likely to disrupt global trade and increase volatility in financial markets, including stock, currency and interest rate markets.'

concerns_observed: Fiscal 2025 is not a like-for-like year. CHEP India Private Limited was acquired on January 8, 2025 and merged into the Company, so the year contains CHEP India only from the acquisition date on the actual basis, while a separate Pro Forma Consolidated Financial Information presents Fiscal 2025 as if the acquisition had completed on April 1, 2024. Revenue from operations is Rs.4,664.72 million actual against Rs.6,210.22 million pro forma; total income Rs.4,850.31 million actual against Rs.6,858.91 million pro forma. Risk Factor 37 states the pro forma information 'addresses a hypothetical situation', was not prepared under any GAAP or accounting standard, and 'the degree of reliance placed on it should be limited'.

The DRHP contradicts itself on the CHEP merger effective date: 'Our Business' states the CHEP Scheme of Merger effective date as January 2, 2025, while Risk Factors and the MD&A state June 2, 2025. The rolled-up extraction store carries only the June 2, 2025 date; the inconsistency is recorded in this run's assembled extract.

The DRHP contradicts itself on the CHEP acquisition completion date: the Risk Factors preamble and Risk Factor 26 state January 8, 2025, while Risk Factor 37 states the acquisition was 'completed on January 7, 2025'. Risk Factor 37 is the risk factor that governs the pro forma presentation, so the date discrepancy sits on the document that defines the pro forma cut-off.

The DRHP prints two different Fiscal 2025 net profit figures: Rs.357.58 million in the Risk Factor 17 growth table and Rs.375.58 million in the MD&A non-GAAP reconciliation. Both are described as 'net profit for the year' for Fiscal 2025; the DRHP does not reconcile them in the extracted text.

The Offer is predominantly secondary. Total Offer up to Rs.24,000.00 million comprises a Fresh Issue of up to Rs.4,000.00 million and an Offer for Sale of up to Rs.20,000.00 million; Vertical Holdings II Pte. Ltd. is selling up to Rs.19,986.23 million and KIA EBT Scheme 3 up to Rs.13.77 million. Risk Factor 42 states the Company will not receive any portion of the Offer for Sale proceeds.

Ownership is near-total: Promoters Sunu Mathew and Vertical Holdings II Pte. Ltd. hold 391,393,072 Equity Shares, being 95.28% of the issued, subscribed and paid-up equity share capital on a fully diluted basis, assuming conversion of 93,129,624 Preference Shares held by Vertical into a maximum of 277,675,832 Equity Shares. Post-Offer promoter holding is left as '[●]'. As on the date of filing the Company has only 11 Shareholders including Equity and Preference Shareholders.

A leveraged promoter share pledge is disclosed in Risk Factor 15: 13,641,713 Equity Shares, 3.32% of pre-Offer fully diluted capital, are pledged in favour of Catalyst Trusteeship Limited (12,429,105 of Sunu Mathew's 87,655,036 shares; 1,212,608 held by Promoter Group entity Matyas Possessiones Private Limited), securing 600 unlisted non-convertible debentures of face value Rs.1,000,000 each issued by Matyas, whose proceeds were used inter alia to finance Matyas's own acquisition of the Company's Equity Shares. The share pledge agreement dated August 21, 2025 is described as unattested.

A very large pre-Offer conversion sits ahead of the Offer: 99,674,311 outstanding Preference Shares will convert into a maximum of up to 289,617,484 equity shares prior to filing of the Red Herring Prospectus, taking pre-Offer capital from 120,730,296 to 410,347,780 equity shares. Every share-count and percentage tied to the Offer itself remains '[●]'.

Return ratios are low against the reported margin. RoNW is 4.09% (Fiscal 2025), 5.21% (Fiscal 2024), 1.58% (Fiscal 2023), and basic EPS fell to Rs.1.00 in Fiscal 2025 (diluted Rs.0.99) from Rs.1.04 in Fiscal 2024 (diluted Rs.1.03) even as revenue from operations grew; NAV per Equity Share is Rs.24.35 as at March 31, 2025.

Capital structure was reworked in the weeks before filing: conversion to a public limited company with a fresh certificate of incorporation dated July 31, 2025, and a bonus issue of three equity shares for every one held on August 8, 2025 (90,547,722 equity shares) — three weeks before the DRHP date of August 29, 2025. Form FC-GPR for the bonus allotment was filed on August 26, 2025 and the Company is awaiting acknowledgment from RBI.

Promoter entry costs differ by an order of magnitude: average cost of acquisition per Equity Share post-conversion is Rs.3.74 for Sunu Mathew, Rs.70.93 for Vertical Holdings II Pte. Ltd. (the Promoter Selling Shareholder) and Rs.52.48 for KIA EBT Scheme 3.

No valuation benchmark is available by the issuer's own affirmative statement: 'We believe there are no listed comparable companies in India or globally in terms of our business and scale of operations. Hence, no suitable industry peers are available based on our analysis of regulatory filings and industry data.' Risk Factor 64 states accordingly that 'any valuation exercise undertaken for the purposes of the Offer by the Company in consultation with the BRLMs would not be based on a benchmark with industry peers', and the price-to-earnings and market-capitalisation multiples are left as '[●]'.

Litigation is concentrated in tax. Against the Company: 67 tax proceedings aggregating Rs.289.64 million. By the Company: 2 material civil litigations aggregating Rs.54.12 million, including a Section 9 arbitration petition dated December 3, 2019 before the High Court of Bombay against Radhakrishna Foodland Private Limited with a claim of Rs.39.73 million. Against the Subsidiary: 5 tax proceedings aggregating Rs.4.66 million. One criminal proceeding is disclosed against a member of Senior Management. The extraction's code-computed rollup puts total litigation at 92.77% of PAT and 3.8% of net worth.

Contingent liabilities stepped up sharply in the merger year: claims against the Group not acknowledged as debt were Rs.90.31 million in Fiscal 2025 (income tax Rs.71.44 million, indirect tax Rs.18.87 million) against Rs.1.09 million in each of Fiscal 2024 and Fiscal 2023 — 0.98% of net worth per the extraction's derivation.

Supplier concentration is high and partly anonymous: top ten suppliers were 60.00% of total purchases in Fiscal 2025 (Rs.2,630.21 million), 77.00% in Fiscal 2024 and 75.11% in Fiscal 2023 off a base of 381 suppliers; the largest, disclosed only as 'Supplier 1^', was Rs.808.92 million / 18.45% of Fiscal 2025 purchases, and the DRHP states the names of certain top 10 suppliers are withheld 'due to non-receipt of consent from these suppliers'.

Working capital lengthened on the actual basis: net working capital days of 100.08 in Fiscal 2025 against 83.38 (Fiscal 2024) and 80.81 (Fiscal 2023); the Fiscal 2025 pro forma figure is 75.17, a different basis. Trade receivables were 42.69% of revenue from operations in Fiscal 2025 actual against 39.35% (Fiscal 2024) and 33.68% (Fiscal 2023), with 32.07% quoted on the pro forma basis.

Fiscal 2025 investing outflows were funded externally: the Restated Consolidated Statement of Cash Flow shows purchase consideration paid towards business combination of Rs.10,041.30 million and purchase of PPE/CWIP/intangibles of Rs.2,934.90 million, against financing inflows including proceeds from issue of preference shares of Rs.7,853.32 million, proceeds from issue of equity shares of Rs.700.00 million and proceeds from long-term borrowings of Rs.4,094.11 million; cash and cash equivalents at year end were Rs.263.93 million, after adding Rs.363.80 million acquired through the business combination.

Leverage remains materially larger than the earmarked repayment: total outstanding borrowings on a consolidated basis were Rs.8,736.17 million as on May 31, 2025, against Rs.3,001.15 million of Net Proceeds earmarked for repayment/prepayment; the itemised loan table in the Objects section separately prints principal outstanding as on May 31, 2025 of Rs.3,156.25 million against sanctioned Rs.4,000.00 million. Risk Factor 9 notes covenants permitting 'conversion of whole or outstanding part of the debt into equity capital of the Company'.

Attrition is elevated across every disclosed category: KMP attrition 67.00% / 67.00% / 33.00%, Senior Management (other than KMPs) 33.00% / 33.00% / 20.00%, permanent employees 36.81% / 48.13% / 40.52%, and MHE operators 47.00% / 65.00% / 77.00% for Fiscals 2025 / 2024 / 2023, against 3 KMPs in each of the three years.

Statutory and secretarial compliance lapses are disclosed: one instance of delayed payment of tax under the Income Tax Act, 1961 of Rs.0.40 million with a 337-day delay in Fiscal 2024, attributed to a mismatch in employees' KYC details; delayed submission of e-form PAS-3 and DIR-12 with additional fees; and form DIR-12 for the appointment and subsequent resignation of one former director is still to be filed as of the DRHP date.

Risk Factor 39 discloses CARO 2020 matters and auditor comments: 'certain disputed dues primarily related to Goods and Services Tax ("GST") across several states, Income Tax, Value Added Tax ("VAT"), Central Sales Tax, and certain custom/excise matters', and 'instances where the audit trail (edit log) was not enabled at the database level for certain periods, and in some cases, the feature was periodically disabled or not available in the software version used'.

Related-party flows through the subsidiary are large, though eliminated on consolidation: loans given to TARON Material Handling Equipments Private Limited of Rs.742.00 million in Fiscal 2025 with a year-end balance of Rs.1,344.25 million against Rs.817.25 million (Fiscal 2024) and Rs.562.88 million (Fiscal 2023); corporate guarantees given of Rs.271.54 million at Fiscal 2025 year-end. The Corporate Promoter also funded the Company directly — Series I CCPS of Rs.3,330.00 million in Fiscal 2025 and Series H CCPS of Rs.1,500.00 million in Fiscal 2024, both to Vertical Holdings II Pte. Ltd.

Two of the six directors are nominees of the Corporate Promoter under the Shareholders' Agreement (Hardik Bhadrik Shah, Vaibhav Vaidya), and Hardik Bhadrik Shah is disclosed as a beneficiary of KIA EBT Scheme 3, one of the Selling Shareholders in the Offer. All three Independent Directors were appointed in 2025 — April 16, 2025, July 17, 2025 and August 14, 2025 — within months of the August 29, 2025 DRHP date.

The Fresh Issue has no growth object: proceeds are limited to repayment/prepayment of borrowings of Rs.3,001.15 million and general corporate purposes shown as '[●]' (capped at 25% of Gross Proceeds), the entire deployment is scheduled in Fiscal 2026, and 'Fund requirements and deployment of funds have not been appraised by any bank or financial institution or any other independent agency'. A monitoring agency is to be appointed only prior to filing of the Red Herring Prospectus.

Revenue remains pallet-weighted and the mix shifts materially between bases: pallet pooling was 67.90% of revenue from operations in Fiscal 2025 actual (Rs.3,167.44 million) against 62.90% pro forma (Rs.3,906.13 million), 72.23% (Fiscal 2024) and 84.14% (Fiscal 2023). Automotive rises from 14.31% of revenue on the Fiscal 2025 actual basis to 24.28% pro forma, while F&B falls from 30.06% to 25.8% — the customer-industry mix on the two Fiscal 2025 bases is not the same business.

Pallet replenishment consumes a large share of revenue: costs incurred towards additions in pallets were Rs.2,017.00 million / 43.24% of total revenue from operations (Fiscal 2025), Rs.1,869.22 million / 51.22% (Fiscal 2024) and Rs.1,171.82 million / 46.25% (Fiscal 2023), while Risk Factor 18 notes that agreements 'typically ... long term agreements up to five years' may prevent timely pass-through of cost increases.

Customer concentration is lower in the most recent year on both bases: top 10 customers were 34.18% of revenue from operations in Fiscal 2025 actual and 28.72% on the Fiscal 2025 pro forma basis, against 39.49% (Fiscal 2024) and 37.77% (Fiscal 2023) actual.

Credit and borrowing record as disclosed: 'a credit/debt rating of A by India Ratings in 2024 and there has been no downgrade to our Company's credit ratings during Fiscals 2025, 2024 and 2023'; 'We have not defaulted on any loans in the financial years ended March 31, 2025, March 31, 2024 and March 31, 2023'; the DRHP states there has been no instance of delays, defaults and rescheduling/restructuring of the borrowings of the Company.

Asset-leakage cost has stayed small relative to the asset base as disclosed: impairment loss on Assets lost and not yet recovered from customers of Rs.52.39 million (Fiscal 2025), Rs.53.52 million (Fiscal 2024), Rs.3.07 million (Fiscal 2023), being 0.43%, 0.55% and 0.04% of net block.
